\label{remark: intro / etale-cup-combinatorial}
  In practice, the object $(\bar\pi_1(X))^{\rm ac}$ can be explicitly computed using cohomology with $\mathbb{Z}/\ell$ coefficients.
  Indeed, for any $X \in \mathbf{Var}_{k_0}$, one has $\pi^a(X) = \operatorname{H}_{\text{\'et}}^1(\bar X,\mathbb{Z}/\ell)^\vee$, and the inclusion $\mathcal{R} := \mathcal{R}(\pi^c(X)) \hookrightarrow \wedge^2 (\pi^a(X))$ is dual to (the image of) 
  \[ \wedge^2 (\operatorname{H}_{\text{\'et}}^1(\bar X,\mathbb{Z}/\ell)) \xrightarrow{\cup} \operatorname{H}_{\text{\'et}}^2(\bar X,\mathbb{Z}/\ell). \]
  In other words, one can completely compute the object $(\bar\pi_1(X))^{\rm ac}$ using the \emph{finite-dimensional} $\mathbb{Z}/\ell$-vector space $\operatorname{H}_{\text{\'et}}^1(\bar X,\mathbb{Z}/\ell)$, along with the kernel of the cup-product map above. 
  In particular, $\mathrm{Aut}^c(\pi^a(X))$ is a subgroup of the \emph{finite group} $\mathrm{Aut}(\pi^a(X)) = \operatorname{GL}_{\mathbb{Z}/\ell}(\pi^a(X))$.
  In this respect, one may view $(\bar\pi_1(X))^{\rm ac}$ as a combinatorial object, defined by a \emph{finite} vector space with some additional linear data.

nodes.statement: Put p = Char F and assume that p > 0. Since L is finite and purely inseparable over F, one has L subset F^1/p^n for sufficiently large n. Since p is invertible in Z/ell, the canonical map k^M_*(F) rightarrow k^M_*(F^1/p^n) is an isomorphism. As this map factors through k^M_*(L), we deduce that the map k^M_*(F) rightarrow k^M_*(L) is injective. To deduce that k^M_*(F) rightarrow k^M_*(L) is also surjective, it suffices to prove that k^M_*(L) rightarrow k^M_*(F^1/p^n) is injective. For any eta in the kernel of k^M_*(L) rightarrow k^M_*(F^1/p^n), there exists some intermediate extension M of F^1/p^n|L such that M|L is finite and such that eta is in the kernel of k^M_*(L) rightarrow k^M_*(M). But such a subextension M|L is purely inseparable, so the argument above shows that eta = 0. Thus k^M_*(L) rightarrow k^M_*(F^1/p^n) is injective, as required.
nodes.raw_latex:
Put $p = \mathrm{Char} F$ and assume that $p > 0$.
  Since $L$ is finite and purely inseparable over $F$, one has $L \subset F^{1/p^n}$ for sufficiently large $n$.
  Since $p$ is invertible in $\mathbb{Z}/\ell$, the canonical map $\operatorname{k}^{\rm M}_*(F) \rightarrow \operatorname{k}^{\rm M}_*(F^{1/p^n})$ is an isomorphism.
  As this map factors through $\operatorname{k}^{\rm M}_*(L)$, we deduce that the map $\operatorname{k}^{\rm M}_*(F) \rightarrow \operatorname{k}^{\rm M}_*(L)$ is injective.
  To deduce that $\operatorname{k}^{\rm M}_*(F) \rightarrow \operatorname{k}^{\rm M}_*(L)$ is also surjective, it suffices to prove that $\operatorname{k}^{\rm M}_*(L) \rightarrow \operatorname{k}^{\rm M}_*(F^{1/p^n})$ is injective.
  
  For any $\eta$ in the kernel of $\operatorname{k}^{\rm M}_*(L) \rightarrow \operatorname{k}^{\rm M}_*(F^{1/p^n})$, there exists some intermediate extension $M$ of $F^{1/p^n}|L$ such that $M|L$ is finite and such that $\eta$ is in the kernel of $\operatorname{k}^{\rm M}_*(L) \rightarrow \operatorname{k}^{\rm M}_*(M)$.
  But such a subextension $M|L$ is purely inseparable, so the argument above shows that $\eta = 0$.
  Thus $\operatorname{k}^{\rm M}_*(L) \rightarrow \operatorname{k}^{\rm M}_*(F^{1/p^n})$ is injective, as required.

But such a subextension M|L is purely inseparable, so the argument above shows that eta = 0. Thus k^M_*(L) rightarrow k^M_*(F^1/p^n) is injective, as required.

\label{fact: milnor / tame / laurent-coords}
  Let $F$ be any field, and let $t_1,\ldots,t_d$ be algebraically independent indeterminants over $F$.
  Consider the field of Laurent series $L = F((t_1,\ldots,t_d))$ over $F$.
  Let $f_0$ be a non-trivial element of $\operatorname{k}^{\rm M}_r(F)$ for some $r \geq 0$, and let $f := \{f_0\}_L$ denote the image of $f_0$ in $\operatorname{k}^{\rm M}_r(L)$.
  Then the product
  \[ \{t_1,\ldots,t_d,f\}_L \]
  is non-trivial in $\operatorname{k}^{\rm M}_{r+d}(L)$.

We proceed to prove this by induction on d, with the base case d = 0 being trivial. For the inductive case, let v be the t_1-adic valuation on L'. Then the residue field of v can be canonically identified with F((t_d))cdots((t_2)) =: M via the obvious map sending t_i in U_v to t_i in M for i geq 2. nodes.statement: As noted above, it suffices to prove assertion (1) as assertions (2) and (3) follow from this. First, note that the Kummer pairing canonically induces a perfect pairing \[ widehatwedge^2(G_K^a) times wedge^2 (k^M_1(K)) rightarrow mu_ell^otimes 2. \] Let R(G_K) denote the kernel of the map \[ [bullet,bullet] : widehatwedge^2(G_K^a) rightarrow G_K^(2)/G_K^(3). \] Since k^M_*(K) is a quadratic Z/ell-algebra, in order to prove assertion (1), it suffices to prove that the dual of the inclusion R(G_K) hookrightarrow widehatwedge^2(G_K^a) with respect to the pairing above is the (surjective) multiplication map \[ wedge^2 (k^M_1(K)) twoheadrightarrow k^M_2(K) \] in the mod-ell Milnor K-ring. This follows easily by combining Fact (3) with the Merkurjev-Suslin Theorem and Fact , as follows. First, since mu_ell subset K, we may simplify the notation and choose a fixed isomorphism mu_ell cong Z/ell of Gal_K-modules. In particular, we may identify k^M_1(K) with H^1(G_K^a) = H^1(G_K) via the Kummer pairing, and k^M_2(K) with H^2(G_K) via the Merkurjev-Suslin Theorem and Fact (2). Next, recall from Fact that the Bockstein morphism beta : H^1(G_K) rightarrow H^2(G_K) is trivial. Hence, the inflation map H^2(G_K^a) rightarrow H^2(G_K) factors through H^2(G_K^a)/betaH^1(G_K^a), which is isomorphic to wedge^2(k^M_1(K)) by Fact and our identification H^1(G_K^a) = k^M_1(K) above. Finally, using the LHS spectral sequence and the fact that H^2(G_K)_dec = H^2(G_K) by the Merkurjev-Suslin Theorem and Fact (2), we have a canonical short exact sequence \[ 0 rightarrow H^1(G_K^(2))^G_K xrightarrowd_2 H^2(G_K^a) rightarrow H^2(G_K) rightarrow 0, \] which induces an exact sequence \[ H^1(G_K^(2)/G_K^(3)) xrightarrow-d_2 wedge^2(H^1(G_K^a)) rightarrow H^2(G_K) rightarrow 0 \] by Fact . Once we identify H^1(G_K^a) with k^M_1(K) and H^2(G_K) with k^M_2(K), the right-hand map of this sequence is precisely the multiplication map. Finally, the dual of this sequence is precisely \[ 0 rightarrow R(G_K) rightarrow widehatwedge^2(G_K^a) xrightarrow[bullet,bullet] G_K^(2)/G_K^(3) \] by Fact (3).

As noted above, it suffices to prove assertion (1) as assertions (2) and (3) follow from this.
  First, note that the Kummer pairing canonically induces a perfect pairing
  \[ \widehat\wedge^2(\mathcal{G}_K^a) \times \wedge^2 (\operatorname{k}^{\rm M}_1(K)) \rightarrow \mu_\ell^{\otimes 2}. \]
  Let $\mathcal{R}(\mathcal{G}_K)$ denote the kernel of the map
  \[ [\bullet,\bullet] : \widehat\wedge^2(\mathcal{G}_K^a) \rightarrow \mathcal{G}_K^{(2)}/\mathcal{G}_K^{(3)}. \]
  Since $\operatorname{k}^{\rm M}_*(K)$ is a quadratic $\mathbb{Z}/\ell$-algebra, in order to prove assertion (1), it suffices to prove that the dual of the inclusion $\mathcal{R}(\mathcal{G}_K) \hookrightarrow \widehat\wedge^2(\mathcal{G}_K^a)$ with respect to the pairing above is the (surjective) multiplication map 
  \[ \wedge^2 (\operatorname{k}^{\rm M}_1(K)) \twoheadrightarrow \operatorname{k}^{\rm M}_2(K) \]
  in the mod-$\ell$ Milnor K-ring.
  This follows easily by combining Fact \ref{fact: cohom / generalities / cup-vs-commutator}(3) with the Merkurjev-Suslin Theorem \cite{Merkurjev:1982} and Fact \ref{fact: cohom / kummer / generalities-kummer}, as follows.
  
  First, since $\mu_\ell \subset K$, we may simplify the notation and choose a fixed isomorphism $\mu_\ell \cong \mathbb{Z}/\ell$ of $\mathrm{Gal}_K$-modules.
  In particular, we may identify $\operatorname{k}^{\rm M}_1(K)$ with $\operatorname{H}^1(\mathcal{G}_K^a) = \operatorname{H}^1(\mathcal{G}_K)$ via the Kummer pairing, and $\operatorname{k}^{\rm M}_2(K)$ with $\operatorname{H}^2(\mathcal{G}_K)$ via the Merkurjev-Suslin Theorem \cite{Merkurjev:1982} and Fact \ref{fact: cohom / kummer / generalities-kummer}(2).

  Next, recall from Fact \ref{fact: cohom / kummer / generalities-kummer} that the Bockstein morphism $\beta : \operatorname{H}^1(\mathcal{G}_K) \rightarrow \operatorname{H}^2(\mathcal{G}_K)$ is trivial.
  Hence, the inflation map $\operatorname{H}^2(\mathcal{G}_K^a) \rightarrow \operatorname{H}^2(\mathcal{G}_K)$ factors through $\operatorname{H}^2(\mathcal{G}_K^a)/\beta\operatorname{H}^1(\mathcal{G}_K^a)$, which is isomorphic to $\wedge^2(\operatorname{k}^{\rm M}_1(K))$ by Fact \ref{fact: cohom / generalities / cup-vs-commutator} and our identification $\operatorname{H}^1(\mathcal{G}_K^a) = \operatorname{k}^{\rm M}_1(K)$ above.

  Finally, using the LHS spectral sequence and the fact that $\operatorname{H}^2(\mathcal{G}_K)_{\rm dec} = \operatorname{H}^2(\mathcal{G}_K)$ by the Merkurjev-Suslin Theorem and Fact \ref{fact: cohom / kummer / generalities-kummer}(2), we have a canonical short exact sequence
  \[ 0 \rightarrow \operatorname{H}^1(\mathcal{G}_K^{(2)})^{\mathcal{G}_K} \xrightarrow{d_2} \operatorname{H}^2(\mathcal{G}_K^a) \rightarrow \operatorname{H}^2(\mathcal{G}_K) \rightarrow 0, \]
  which induces an exact sequence
  \[ \operatorname{H}^1(\mathcal{G}_K^{(2)}/\mathcal{G}_K^{(3)}) \xrightarrow{-d_2} \wedge^2(\operatorname{H}^1(\mathcal{G}_K^a)) \rightarrow \operatorname{H}^2(\mathcal{G}_K) \rightarrow 0 \]
  by Fact \ref{fact: cohom / generalities / cup-vs-commutator}.
  Once we identify $\operatorname{H}^1(\mathcal{G}_K^a)$ with $\operatorname{k}^{\rm M}_1(K)$ and $\operatorname{H}^2(\mathcal{G}_K)$ with $\operatorname{k}^{\rm M}_2(K)$, the right-hand map of this sequence is precisely the multiplication map.
  Finally, the dual of this sequence is precisely 
  \[ 0 \rightarrow \mathcal{R}(\mathcal{G}_K) \rightarrow \widehat\wedge^2(\mathcal{G}_K^a) \xrightarrow{[\bullet,\bullet]} \mathcal{G}_K^{(2)}/\mathcal{G}_K^{(3)} \]
  by Fact \ref{fact: cohom / generalities / cup-vs-commutator}(3).

Before we begin the proof, we choose an isomorphism $\mu_\ell \cong \mathbb{Z}/\ell$ which will be fixed throughout, and which allows us to identify $\mathcal{G}_K^a$ with $\mathfrak{g}(K)$ by Kummer theory.

  \vskip 5pt
  \emph{Proof of (1):}
  Let $\sigma^*$ denote the element of $\mathrm{Aut}^{\rm c}(\mathcal{G}_K^a)$ which is the dual of $\sigma$ under the Kummer pairing (see Theorem \ref{theorem: cohom / kummer / galois-to-milnor}(1)).
  Recall that $\mathfrak{U}_v$ resp. $\mathfrak{U}_v^1$ is the orthogonal of $\mathrm{I}_v$ resp. $\mathrm{D}_v$ under this Kummer pairing
  \[ \mathcal{G}_K^a \times \operatorname{k}^{\rm M}_1(K) \rightarrow \mu_\ell \cong \mathbb{Z}/\ell. \]
  Therefore, it suffices to show that there exists an $r$-quasi-divisorial valuation $v^\sigma$ such that
  \[ \sigma^*\mathrm{I}_v = \mathrm{I}_{v^\sigma}, \ \ \sigma^*\mathrm{D}_v = \mathrm{D}_{v^\sigma}, \]
  as the uniqueness of this $v^\sigma$ will be discussed at the end of the proof.

  Recall from Theorem \ref{theorem: cohom / kummer / galois-to-milnor}(1) that $\sigma^*$ is compatible with $\mathcal{R}$, hence $\sigma^*$ is compatible with C-pairs by Fact \ref{fact: localthy / c-pairs / c-vs-cl}.
  The proof now proceeds by induction on $r$.
  The base case $r = 1$ follows immediately from \cite{Topaz:2015}*{Theorem D} and/or \cite{Pop:2010a}*{Theorem 1}.

  The inductive case proceeds as follows.
  First, write an $r$-quasi-divisorial valuation $v$ as $v = w \circ w_0$ with $w_0$ an $(r-1)$-quasi-divisorial valuation and $w$ a quasi-divisorial valuation of $Kw_0|kw_0$.
  By induction, there exists an $(r-1)$-quasi-divisorial valuation $w_1 = w_0^\sigma$ such that
  \[ \sigma^* \mathrm{D}_{w_0} = \mathrm{D}_{w_1},\ \ \sigma^*\mathrm{I}_{w_0} = \mathrm{I}_{w_1}. \]
  Thus, $\sigma^*$ induces an isomorphism
  \[ \sigma^* : \mathfrak{g}(Kw_0) = \mathrm{D}_{w_0}/\mathrm{I}_{w_0} \xrightarrow{\cong} \mathrm{D}_{w_1}/\mathrm{I}_{w_1} = \mathfrak{g}(Kw_1) \]
  by Fact \ref{fact: localthy / mindec / mindec}.
  Also, note that $tr.deg(Kw_0|kw_0) \geq 2$ by assumption.
  By Fact \ref{fact: localthy / mindec / c-pair-mindec}, this isomorphism $\sigma^* : \mathfrak{g}(Kw_0) \rightarrow \mathfrak{g}(Kw_1)$ is compatible with C-pairs.
  Using \cite{Topaz:2015}*{Theorem D} again, it follows that there exists a quasi-divisorial valuation $w'$ of $Kw_1|kw_1$ such that $\sigma^* \mathrm{I}_w = \mathrm{I}_{w'}$ and $\sigma^* \mathrm{D}_w = \mathrm{D}_{w'}$.
  Letting $v^\sigma := w' \circ w_1$, it follows from Fact \ref{fact: localthy / mindec / mindec} that $\sigma^* \mathrm{I}_v = \mathrm{I}_{v^\sigma}$ and $\sigma^*\mathrm{D}_w = \mathrm{D}_{v^\sigma}$, as required.

  \vskip 5pt
  \emph{Proof of (2):}
  Since $vK$ and $wK$ contain no non-trivial $\ell$-divisible convex subgroups, it follows from \cite{Topaz:2015}*{Lemma 3.1} or \cite{Topaz:2013a}*{Lemma 3.4} that $v$ is a coarsening of $w$ if and only if $\mathrm{I}_v \subset \mathrm{I}_w$.
  By assertion (1), this is true if and only if $\mathrm{I}_{v^\sigma} \subset \mathrm{I}_{w^\sigma}$, which is similarly equivalent to $v^\sigma$ being a coarsening of $w^\sigma$.
  This observation also implies that $v^\sigma$ is uniquely determined by $v$ and by $\sigma$.

nodes.statement: First of all, note that K|K_0 and k|k_0 are both algebraic extensions. Thus, the associated residue extensions, Kv|K_0v and kv|k_0v, are also algebraic. Moreover, since k is algebraically closed, the residue field kv is also algebraically closed. In particular, if tr.deg(Kv|kv) geq 1, then K_0v cannot be contained in kv, and therefore there exist (many) elements t in U_v cap K_0^times whose image bar t in Kv is transcendental over kv. Now assume that v is r-divisorial, hence v is trivial on k. Since r < tr.deg(K|k), it follows that Kv is a function field of transcendence degree geq 1 over k. Arguing as above, we see that there exists some element \[ t in (U_v cap K_0^times) smallsetminus k_0 \] such that the image bar t of t in Kv is transcendental over k. This implies that K(t)^times subset U_v and that the image of K(t) in Kv is a function field of transcendence degree 1 over k. Let L' denote the image of K(t) in Kv and let L denote the relative algebraic closure of L' in Kv. Note that L is a finite extension of L', and that K(t) rightarrow L' is an isomorphism. If we consider the canonical map \[ K(t) hookrightarrow U_v twoheadrightarrow U_v / U_v^1 = k^M_1(Kv) \] then its kernel is the same as the kernel of K(t) cong k^M_1(L') rightarrow k^M_1(L), which is finite by Kummer theory. On the other hand, this kernel is precisely U_v^1 cap K(t). Conversely, assume that v is not r-divisorial, hence v is non-trivial on k, and let t in K_0 smallsetminus k_0 be given. We must show that K(t) cap U_v^1 is infinite. By replacing t with t^-1 if needed, we may assume, without loss of generality, that v(t) geq 0. Now let a in k^times be any element such that v(a) < 0. For all such a, one has v(a^-1 t) > 0, and therefore \[ \a-t\_K = \1-a^-1t\_K in U_v^1 cap K(t).\] On the other hand, there are infinitely many such a in k^times, hence the set \[ \\a-t\_k(t) \ : \ a in k^times, \ v(a) < 0 \ \] is an infinite linearly-independent subset of k^M_1(k(t)). Since the map given by the composition k^M_1(k(t)) rightarrow k^M_1(K(t)) cong K(t) has a finite kernel by Kummer theory, it follows that U_v^1 cap K(t) is infinite, as required.

  Now assume that $v$ is $r$-divisorial, hence $v$ is trivial on $k$.
  Since $r < tr.deg(K|k)$, it follows that $Kv$ is a function field of transcendence degree $\geq 1$ over $k$.
  Arguing as above, we see that there exists some element
  \[ t \in ({\rm U}_v \cap K_0^\times) \smallsetminus k_0 \]
  such that the image $\bar t$ of $t$ in $Kv$ is transcendental over $k$.
  This implies that $\mathbb{K}(t)^\times \subset {\rm U}_v$ and that the image of $\mathbb{K}(t)$ in $Kv$ is a function field of transcendence degree $1$ over $k$.
  Let $L'$ denote the image of $\mathbb{K}(t)$ in $Kv$ and let $L$ denote the relative algebraic closure of $L'$ in $Kv$.
  Note that $L$ is a finite extension of $L'$, and that $\mathbb{K}(t) \rightarrow L'$ is an isomorphism.

  If we consider the canonical map
  \[ \mathfrak{K}(t) \hookrightarrow \mathfrak{U}_v \twoheadrightarrow \mathfrak{U}_v / \mathfrak{U}_v^1 = \operatorname{k}^{\rm M}_1(Kv) \]
  then its kernel is the same as the kernel of $\mathfrak{K}(t) \cong \operatorname{k}^{\rm M}_1(L') \rightarrow \operatorname{k}^{\rm M}_1(L)$, which is finite by Kummer theory.
  On the other hand, this kernel is precisely $\mathfrak{U}_v^1 \cap \mathfrak{K}(t)$.

  Conversely, assume that $v$ is not $r$-divisorial, hence $v$ is non-trivial on $k$, and let $t \in K_0 \smallsetminus k_0$ be given.
  We must show that $\mathfrak{K}(t) \cap \mathfrak{U}_v^1$ is infinite.
  By replacing $t$ with $t^{-1}$ if needed, we may assume, without loss of generality, that $v(t) \geq 0$.

  Now let $a \in k^\times$ be any element such that $v(a) < 0$.
  For all such $a$, one has $v(a^{-1} t) > 0$, and therefore
  \[ \{a-t\}_K = \{1-a^{-1}t\}_K \in \mathfrak{U}_v^1 \cap \mathfrak{K}(t).\]

  \[ \mathrm{cl}(S) = \{A \in \mathbb{G}^1(L|F) \ : \ A \leq \vee S\}. \]

  Conversely, given the set $\mathbb{G}^1(L|F)$ endowed with the closure operation $\mathrm{cl}$ defined above, it is easy to see that $\mathbb{G}^*(L|F)$ is canonically isomorphic to the \emph{lattice of flats} associated to the combinatorial geometry $(\mathbb{G}^1(L|F),\mathrm{cl})$.

  where $\mathrm{Aut}^{\mathrm{cl}}(\mathbb{G}^1(L|F))$ denotes the set of permutations of $\mathbb{G}^1(L|F)$ which are compatible with the closure operation $\mathrm{cl}$.

nodes.statement: We first use Theorem to make the following observation: Any automorphism Phi of G^*(K|k) arises from an automorphism tildePhi of K^i which is unique up-to composition with some power of Frob_K^i. Assume moreover that Phi restricts to an automorphism Phi_0 of G^*(K_0|k_0). Then Theorem implies that Phi_0 arises from an automorphism tildePhi_0 of K_0^i which is unique up-to composition with some power of Frob_K_0^i. It therefore follows from the functoriality of the situation that this automorphism tildePhi restricts to an automorphism of K_0^i, which is precisely tildePhi_0, up-to composition with a power of Frob_K_0^i. Consider the following subgroup of Aut_\K_0^i\(K^i): \[ G:= \sigma in Aut_\K_0^i\(K^i) \ : \ sigma|_K_0^i in langle Frob_K_0^i rangle \.\] By Theorem and the observations made above, we see that the canonical map \[ G rightarrow Aut^*(G^*(K|k)|K_0) \] is surjective, and its kernel is the subgroup generated by Frob_K^i. On the other hand, it is easy to see that one has a canonical isomorphism \[ Gal(K|K_0) = Gal(K^i|K_0^i) xrightarrowcong G/langle Frob_K^i rangle. \] Finally, we conclude the proof by recalling that the canonical map rho_k_0 : Gal_k_0 rightarrow Gal(K|K_0) is an isomorphism, since K_0|k_0 is a regular function field. As the isomorphisms \[ Gal(K|K_0) cong G/langle Frob_K^i rangle cong Aut^*(G^*(K|k)|K_0) \] are all compatible with rho_k_0, the assertion follows.

We first use Theorem \ref{theorem: lattice / acl / fund-thm-field-acl} to make the following observation:
  Any automorphism $\Phi$ of $\mathbb{G}^*(K|k)$ arises from an automorphism $\tilde\Phi$ of $K^i$ which is unique up-to composition with some power of $\operatorname{Frob}_{K^i}$.
  Assume moreover that $\Phi$ restricts to an automorphism $\Phi_0$ of $\mathbb{G}^*(K_0|k_0)$.
  Then Theorem \ref{theorem: lattice / acl / fund-thm-field-acl} implies that $\Phi_0$ arises from an automorphism $\tilde\Phi_0$  of $K_0^i$ which is unique up-to composition with some power of $\operatorname{Frob}_{K_0^i}$.
  It therefore follows from the functoriality of the situation that this automorphism $\tilde\Phi$ restricts to an automorphism of $K_0^i$, which is precisely $\tilde\Phi_0$, up-to composition with a power of $\operatorname{Frob}_{K_0^i}$.

  Consider the following subgroup of $\mathrm{Aut}_{\{K_0^i\}}(K^i)$:
  \[ G:= \{\sigma \in \mathrm{Aut}_{\{K_0^i\}}(K^i) \ : \ \sigma|_{K_0^i} \in \langle \operatorname{Frob}_{K_0^i} \rangle \}.\]
  By Theorem \ref{theorem: lattice / acl / fund-thm-field-acl} and the observations made above, we see that the canonical map
  \[ G \rightarrow \mathrm{Aut}^*(\mathbb{G}^*(K|k)|K_0) \]
  is \emph{surjective}, and its kernel is the subgroup generated by $\operatorname{Frob}_{K^i}$.

  On the other hand, it is easy to see that one has a canonical isomorphism
  \[ \mathrm{Gal}(K|K_0) = \mathrm{Gal}(K^i|K_0^i) \xrightarrow{\cong} G/\langle \operatorname{Frob}_{K^i} \rangle. \]
  Finally, we conclude the proof by recalling that the canonical map $\rho_{k_0} : {\mathrm{Gal}_{k_0}} \rightarrow \mathrm{Gal}(K|K_0)$ is an isomorphism, since $K_0|k_0$ is a regular function field.
  As the isomorphisms 
  \[ \mathrm{Gal}(K|K_0) \cong G/\langle \operatorname{Frob}_{K^i} \rangle \cong \mathrm{Aut}^*(\mathbb{G}^*(K|k)|K_0) \]
  are all compatible with $\rho_{k_0}$, the assertion follows.

nodes.statement: As mentioned above, we only need to prove assertion (2) since assertion (1) can be found in *Ch. VIII, pg. 213. To simplify the notation, for P = (a,b) in F^2, we write \[ t_a,b = t_P = fracx-ay-b. \] Since y is separable in L|F, there exists an F-derivation D of L such that D(y) neq 0. Now we may calculate: \[ D(t_a,b) = fracD(x) cdot (y-b) - D(y) cdot (x-a)(y-b)^2. \] Hence D(t_a,b) = 0 if and only if t_a,b = D(x)/D(y), so this can only happen for at most one pair P_0 in F^2. Thus, for any pair (a,b) different from this (possible) exceptional one P_0, the element t_a,b is separable in L|F, which implies that L|F(t_a,b) has a separating transcendence base. For each P in F^2, write E_P := F(t_P) and E'_P for the relative algebraic closure of E_P in L. If P,Q are two different points of F^2, note that one has E_P cdot E_Q = F(x,y). Note that E_P' and E_Q' are regular of transcendence degree 1 over F, since they are contained in L which is regular over F. This implies that E_P' and E_Q' are linearly disjoint over F, since L|F is regular. Let M denote the relative algebraic closure of F(x,y) in L, and note that there are only finitely many intermediate subextensions of M|F(x,y). In particular, there are finitely many subextensions of M|F(x,y) of the form E'_P(x,y). Let P_1,ldots,P_n be finitely many points in F^2 such that E'_P_i(x,y) exhaust all such subextensions. Now suppose that Q is any point of F^2 which is different from P_0,ldots,P_n. Since Q neq P_0, we see that E'_Q is the separable algebraic closure of E_Q in M. Moreover, by the discussion above, E'_Q(x,y) must be linearly disjoint from E'_P_i(x,y) over F(x,y), for all i = 1,ldots,n. This forces E'_Q(x,y) to be precisely F(x,y), and therefore E'_Q = E_Q. In other words, E_Q = F(t_Q) is algebraically closed in L, and since Q neq P_0, we see that L is regular over E_Q = F(t_Q), as required.

nodes.statement: By Lemma (2), there exists a non-empty open subset U_1 of A^2_k such that for all (a,b) in U_1(k), the element t_a,b = (x-a)/(y-b) is general in K|k. We must therefore prove that the second condition for a strongly-general element is also an open condition on (a,b) in A^2_k(k) as above. Put x = t_1, y = t_2 and extend t_1,t_2 to a transcendence base t = (t_1,ldots,t_d) for K|k. Furthermore, consider the canonical coordinate projection A^d_t rightarrow A^2_t_1,t_2. Also, identify A^2_k as above with A^2_t_1,t_2, so that we may consider U_1 as an open subset of A^2_t_1,t_2. Finally, note that K is a finite extension of k(t) = k(A^d_t). Thus, there exists a non-empty open subset U of U_1 such that for all (a,b) in U(k), the fiber of A^d_t rightarrow A^2_t_1,t_2 over the point (a,b) is essentially unramified in K. We will show that this open set U satisfies the required assertion. Let (a,b) in U(k) be given, and consider the (rational) projection A^2_t_1,t_2 rightarrow P^1_t induced by sending t to (x-a)/(y-b). The fibers of this morphism are all lines in A^2_t_1,t_2 given by equations of the form \[ c cdot (x-a) = d cdot (y-b) \] for (c:d) in P^1(k) (written in homogeneous coordinates). All such lines pass through the point (a,b) in A^2_t_1,t_2 hence the fibers of the composition \[ A^d_t rightarrow A^2_t_1,t_2 rightarrow P^1_t \] are all non-empty, geometrically integral, and essentially unramified in K. Let Z be the preimage of (a,b) under the coordinate projection A^d_t twoheadrightarrow A^2_t_1,t_2, and put X:= A^d_t smallsetminus Z. Then the surjective rational morphism A^d_t twoheadrightarrow P^1_t defined above is regular on X, and the induced (regular) map X rightarrow P^1_t is a smooth surjective morphism with geometrically integral fibers. With this set-up, the fact that D_t rightarrow D_t is surjective follows from Lemma , by taking X as above, S = P^1_t, and X rightarrow S the map defined above.

By Lemma \ref{lemma: strgen / general / gen-birat-bertini}(2), there exists a non-empty open subset $U_1$ of $\mathbb{A}^2_k$ such that for all $(a,b) \in U_1(k)$, the element $t_{a,b} = (x-a)/(y-b)$ is general in $K|k$.
  We must therefore prove that the second condition for a strongly-general element is also an open condition on $(a,b) \in \mathbb{A}^2_k(k)$ as above.

  Put $x = t_1$, $y = t_2$ and extend $t_1,t_2$ to a transcendence base $\mathbf{t} = (t_1,\ldots,t_d)$ for $K|k$.
  Furthermore, consider the canonical coordinate projection $\mathbb{A}^d_{\mathbf{t}} \rightarrow \mathbb{A}^2_{t_1,t_2}$.
  Also, identify $\mathbb{A}^2_k$ as above with $\mathbb{A}^2_{t_1,t_2}$, so that we may consider $U_1$ as an open subset of $\mathbb{A}^2_{t_1,t_2}$.
  Finally, note that $K$ is a finite extension of $k(\mathbf{t}) = k(\mathbb{A}^d_{\mathbf{t}})$.
  Thus, there exists a non-empty open subset $U$ of $U_1$ such that for all $(a,b) \in U(k)$, the fiber of $\mathbb{A}^d_{\mathbf{t}} \rightarrow \mathbb{A}^2_{t_1,t_2}$ over the point $(a,b)$ is essentially unramified in $K$.

  \[ c \cdot (x-a) = d \cdot (y-b) \]
  for $(c:d) \in \mathbb{P}^1(k)$ (written in homogeneous coordinates).
  All such lines pass through the point $(a,b)$ in $\mathbb{A}^2_{t_1,t_2}$ hence the fibers of the composition
  \[ \mathbb{A}^d_{\mathbf{t}} \rightarrow \mathbb{A}^2_{t_1,t_2} \rightarrow \mathbb{P}^1_t \]
  are all non-empty, geometrically integral, and essentially unramified in $K$.

nodes.statement: It suffices to prove that every transcendental element x of L is a product of finitely many elements of L which are strongly-general in K|k. Since L is relatively algebraically closed in K, it follows that every non-constant element of L is a power of some element of L which is separable in K|k. Thus, we may assume without loss of generality that x is separable. Moreover, since tr.deg(L|k cap L) = tr.deg(L|k_0) geq 2, there exists another element y in L which is algebraically independent from x over k, and such that y is separable in K|k. Note that if (t-ab)/(u-b) is strongly-general in K|k with a,b in k, then so is \[ fract-abu-b - a = fract-auu-b. \] Thus, using Proposition , the fact that k_0 is infinite, and the assumption that k_0 subset L, we can find a,b in k_0 such that both \[ fracx-ay-b, \ fracxy-bxx-a in L^times \] are strongly-general in K|k. But then we see that \[ x = fracx-ay-b cdot fracxy-bxx-a \] is a product of two elements of L which are strongly-general in K|k. This concludes the proof of the lemma.
nodes.raw_latex:
It suffices to prove that every \emph{transcendental} element $x$ of $L$ is a product of finitely many elements of $L$ which are strongly-general in $K|k$.
  Since $L$ is relatively algebraically closed in $K$, it follows that every non-constant element of $L$ is a power of some element of $L$ which is separable in $K|k$.
  Thus, we may assume without loss of generality that $x$ is separable.
  Moreover, since $tr.deg(L|k \cap L) = tr.deg(L|k_0) \geq 2$, there exists another element $y \in L$ which is algebraically independent from $x$ over $k$, and such that $y$ is separable in $K|k$.

  Note that if $(t-ab)/(u-b)$ is strongly-general in $K|k$ with $a,b \in k$, then so is
  \[ \frac{t-ab}{u-b} - a = \frac{t-au}{u-b}. \]
  Thus, using Proposition \ref{proposition: strgen / strgen / strgen-birat-bertini}, the fact that $k_0$ is infinite, and the assumption that $k_0 \subset L$, we can find $a,b \in k_0$ such that both
  \[ \frac{x-a}{y-b}, \ \frac{xy-bx}{x-a} \in L^\times \]
  are strongly-general in $K|k$.
  But then we see that
  \[ x = \frac{x-a}{y-b} \cdot \frac{xy-bx}{x-a} \]
  is a product of two elements of $L$ which are strongly-general in $K|k$.
  This concludes the proof of the lemma.

The implication $(1) \Rightarrow (2)$ is trivial.
  The proof of the non-trivial direction $(2) \Rightarrow (1)$ has three main steps:
  \begin{enumerate}
    \item First, we show that for all $t \in K \smallsetminus k$ and for all $\mathfrak{V} \in \mathfrak{D}_t$, one has $\sigma \mathfrak{V} = \mathfrak{V}$.
    \item Second, we show that for all $t$ which is strongly-general in $K|k$, the restriction of $\sigma$ to $\mathfrak{K} := \mathfrak{K}(t)$ is of the form $\epsilon_{\mathfrak{K}} \cdot \mathbf{1}_{\mathfrak{K}}$, for some $\epsilon_{\mathfrak{K}} \in (\mathbb{Z}/\ell)^\times$, which \emph{a priori} might depend on $\mathfrak{K}$.
    \item Finally, we show that $\epsilon_{\mathfrak{K}}$ from step (2) doesn't actually depend on $\mathfrak{K}$, and then conclude the proof of the proposition by using Lemma \ref{lemma: strgen / strgen / strgen-generate}.
  \end{enumerate}

  \vskip 5pt
  \noindent\emph{Step (1):} Let $v$ be a divisorial valuation of $K|k$.
  Since $Kv$ is a function field of transcendence degree $\geq 1$ over $k$, it is easy to see that ${\rm U}_v$ is multiplicatively generated by elements $x \in {\rm U}_v$ whose image in $Kv$ is transcendental over $k$.
  For all such $x \in {\rm U}_v$, one has $\mathbb{K}(x)^\times \subset {\rm U}_v$.
  Thus, $\mathfrak{U}_v$ is generated by subgroups of the form $\mathfrak{K}(x)$ such that $\mathfrak{K}(x) \subset \mathfrak{U}_v$.
  Since $\sigma \mathfrak{K}(x) = \mathfrak{K}(x)$ for all $x \in K \smallsetminus k$, it follows that $\sigma \mathfrak{U}_v = \mathfrak{U}_v$.
  For any $t \in K \smallsetminus k$, it follows that $\sigma \mathfrak{V} = \mathfrak{V}$ for all $\mathfrak{V} \in \mathfrak{D}_t$ by the definition of the elements of $\mathfrak{D}_t$.

  \vskip 5pt
  \noindent\emph{Step (2):}
  Let $t$ be strongly-general in $K|k$ and put $\mathfrak{K} = \mathfrak{K}(t)$.
  Consider the canonical rational-like collection $\Psi = (\Psi_{\mathfrak{V}})_{\mathfrak{V} \in \mathfrak{D}_t}$ associated to $\mathbb{K}(t) = k(t)$.
  Since $\sigma \mathfrak{V} = \mathfrak{V}$ for all $\mathfrak{V} \in \mathfrak{D}_t$, we obtain an induced rational-like collection $\Phi = (\Phi_{\mathfrak{V}})_{\mathfrak{V} \in \mathfrak{D}_t}$, where $\Phi_{\mathfrak{V}} := \Psi_{\mathfrak{V}} \circ \sigma$.
  By Lemma \ref{lemma: strgen / rational-like / rational-like}, there exists some $\epsilon_{\mathfrak{K}} \in (\mathbb{Z}/\ell)^\times$ depending only on $\mathfrak{K}$ and $\sigma$, such that $\Phi_{\mathfrak{V}} = \epsilon_{\mathfrak{K}} \cdot \Psi_{\mathfrak{V}}$ for all $\mathfrak{V} \in \mathfrak{D}_t$.
  In other words, for all $x \in \mathfrak{K}$, one has
  \[ \mathrm{div}_\Psi(\sigma x) = \mathrm{div}_\Phi(x) = \epsilon_{\mathfrak{K}} \cdot \mathrm{div}_\Psi(x) = \mathrm{div}_\Psi(\epsilon_{\mathfrak{K}} \cdot x). \]
  The injectivity of $\mathrm{div}_\Psi$ in the definition of $\Psi$ being a rational-like collection implies that $\sigma|_{\mathfrak{K}} = \epsilon_{\mathfrak{K}} \cdot \mathbf{1}_{\mathfrak{K}}$.

  \vskip 5pt
  \noindent\emph{Step (3):}
  Let $t_1,t_2$ be strongly-general in $K|k$, and put $\mathfrak{K}_i := \mathfrak{K}(t_i)$ and $\epsilon_i := \epsilon_{\mathfrak{K}_i}$ for $i = 1,2$.
  If $t_1,t_2$ are algebraically dependent over $k$, then $\mathfrak{K}(t_1) = \mathfrak{K}(t_2)$, so that $\epsilon_1 = \epsilon_2$.

  Assume, on the other hand, that $t_1,t_2$ are algebraically independent over $k$.
  Since $t_i$ is general in $K|k$, we see that $\{\{t_i-a\}_K \ : \ a \in k\}$ is a linearly-independent subset of $\operatorname{k}^{\rm M}_1(K)$.
  Thus, by Proposition \ref{proposition: strgen / strgen / strgen-birat-bertini}, we may choose $a,b \in k$ such that $\{t_1-a\}_K$ and $\{t_2-b\}_K$ are $\mathbb{Z}/\ell$-independent in $\operatorname{k}^{\rm M}_1(K)$ and such that $t_0 := (t_1-a)/(t_2-b)$ is strongly-general in $K|k$.
  Put $\mathfrak{K}_0 = \mathfrak{K}(t_0)$ and $\epsilon_0 = \epsilon_{\mathfrak{K}_0}$.

  We can now calculate:
  \[ \epsilon_0 \cdot (\{t_1-a\}_K - \{t_2-b\}_K) = \sigma \left\{\frac{t_1-a}{t_2-b}\right\}_K = \epsilon_1 \cdot \{t_1-a\}_K - \epsilon_2 \cdot \{t_2-b\}_K.\]
  Since $\{t_1-a\}_K$ and $\{t_2-b\}_K$ are linearly independent in $\operatorname{k}^{\rm M}_1(K)$, it follows that $\epsilon_1 = \epsilon_2 = \epsilon_0$.
  This proves that $\epsilon_{\mathfrak{K}}$ doesn't depend on $\mathfrak{K} = \mathfrak{K}(t)$ for $t$ strongly-general in $K|k$.

  Letting $\epsilon = \epsilon_{\mathfrak{K}}$ for some (hence any) $\mathfrak{K} = \mathfrak{K}(t)$ with $t$ strongly-general, we deduce that $\sigma|_{\mathfrak{K}} = \epsilon \cdot \mathbf{1}|_{\mathfrak{K}}$ for all $\mathfrak{K} = \mathfrak{K}(t)$ with $t$ strongly-general.
  By Lemma \ref{lemma: strgen / strgen / strgen-generate}, we see that $\operatorname{k}^{\rm M}_1(K)$ is generated by its subgroups of the form $\mathfrak{K}(t)$ for $t$ strongly-general in $K|k$. 
  Hence $\sigma = \epsilon \cdot \mathbf{1}_{\operatorname{k}^{\rm M}_1(K)}$, as required.

By replacing $t$ with another element of $K_0$ which generates $\mathbb{K}(t) = k(t)$ over $k$, it suffices to prove that $\tau\mathfrak{V}[t;\infty] = \mathfrak{V}[t;\infty]$.
   By Fact \ref{fact: mainproof / autm-condition}(2), we know that
   \[ \tau\{t\}_K \in \langle\{t\}_K,\{t-a_1\}_K,\ldots,\{t-a_r\}_K \rangle. \]

   By combining Lemmas \ref{lemma: mainproof / K0 / fix-Kfrakt0} and \ref{lemma: mainproof / K0 / divs-local-thy} with the definition of $\mathfrak{D}_t$, it follows that for all $\mathfrak{V} \in \mathfrak{D}_t$, one has $\tau \mathfrak{V} \in \mathfrak{D}_t$ as well.
   In other words, $\mathfrak{V} \mapsto \tau\mathfrak{V}$ can be considered as a permutation of $\mathfrak{D}_t$.

   Note that the $\mathfrak{D}_t$-support of any element of
   \[ \langle\{t\}_K,\{t-a_1\}_K,\ldots,\{t-a_r\}_K \rangle\]
   is contained in the set
   \[ \{\mathfrak{V}[t;0],\mathfrak{V}[t;a_1],\ldots,\mathfrak{V}[t;a_r],\mathfrak{V}[t;\infty]\}. \]
   And since the $\mathfrak{D}_t$-support of $\{t\}_K$ is $\{\mathfrak{V}[t;0],\mathfrak{V}[t;\infty]\}$, it follows that one has
   \[ \tau\mathfrak{V}[t;0] \in \{\mathfrak{V}[t;0],\mathfrak{V}[t;a_1],\ldots,\mathfrak{V}[t;a_r],\mathfrak{V}[t;\infty]\}.\]

   For $c \in k_0^\times$ and $a \in k$, one has $\mathfrak{V}[t/c;a] = \mathfrak{V}[t;ca]$; in particular $\mathfrak{V}[t;0] = \mathfrak{V}[t/c;0]$ for all $c \in k_0^\times$.
   By varying $c \in k_0^\times$ and using the fact that $k_0$ is infinite, we deduce that
   \[ \tau\mathfrak{V}[t;0] \in \bigcap_{c \in k_0^\times}  \{\mathfrak{V}[t;0],\mathfrak{V}[t;ca_1],\ldots,\mathfrak{V}[t;ca_r],\mathfrak{V}[t;\infty]\} = \{\mathfrak{V}[t;0],\mathfrak{V}[t;\infty]\}. \]
   By replacing $t$ with $t^{-1}$, it follows similarly that
   \[ \tau\mathfrak{V}[t;\infty] \in \{\mathfrak{V}[t;0],\mathfrak{V}[t;\infty]\}\]
   as well.
   Hence $\tau$ restricts to a permutation of $\{\mathfrak{V}[t;0],\mathfrak{V}[t;\infty]\}$.

   Finally, for $c \in k_0$, one has $\mathfrak{V}[t-c;0] = \mathfrak{V}[t;c]$.
   Repeating the argument above with $t-c$ for $c \in k_0$, we deduce that
   \[ \tau\mathfrak{V}[t;c] \in \{\mathfrak{V}[t;c],\mathfrak{V}[t;\infty]\}\]
   for all $c \in k_0$.
   But since $\mathfrak{V}[t;c] \neq \mathfrak{V}[t;0]$ for $c \in k_0^\times$ (since $t$ is strongly-general in $K|k$), it follows that $\tau\mathfrak{V}[t;\infty] = \mathfrak{V}[t;\infty]$, as required.

nodes.statement: First, let us assume that t in K_0smallsetminus k_0 is strongly-general in K|k. Recall that the following hold: item First, tau K(t) = K(t) by Lemma . item Second, one has tau V in D_t for all V in D_t by Lemma and the definition of D_t. item Third, for all c in k_0 cup \infty\ = P^1(k_0), one has tauV[t;c] = V[t;c] by Lemma . In particular, tau induces isomorphisms tau : K(t)/V xrightarrowcong K(t)/tauV for every V in D_t. Let Psi = (Psi_V)_V in D_t be the canonical rational-like collection associated to K(t)|k, as defined in S. Consider the induced rational-like collection Psi^tau = (Psi^tau_V)_V in D_t, where the isomorphism Psi^tau_tauV : K(t)/tauV xrightarrowcongZ/ell indexed by tauV is the unique one making the following diagram commute: \[ xymatrix K(t) ar[d]_tau ar@->>[r] & K(t)/V ar[d]_tau ar[r]^-Psi_V & Z/ell ar@=[d] \\ K(t) ar@->>[r] & K(t)/tauV ar[r]_-Psi^tau_tauV & Z/ell. \] By Lemma , there exists an epsilon_t in (Z/ell)^times such that epsilon_t cdot Psi_tauV = Psi^tau_tauV for all V in D_t. Since it will be used later on, recall that this epsilon_t only depends on K(t) and tau. vskip 5pt noindentProof of (1): Now let c in k_0 be given. Then one has div_Psi(\t-c\_K) = [V[t;c]] - [V[t;infty]] since Psi is the canonical rational-like collection associated to K(t). By Lemma , one has tauV[t;c] = V[t;c] and tauV[t;infty] = V[t;infty]. And since Psi^tau_tauV = epsilon_t cdot Psi_tauV for all V in D_t, we deduce that \[ div_Psi(tau\t-c\_K) = div_Psi^tau(\t-c\_K) = epsilon_t cdot [V[t;c]] - epsilon_t cdot [V[t;infty]] = div_Psi(epsilon_t cdot \t-c\_K). \] The injectivity of div_Psi implies that tau\t-c\_K = epsilon_t cdot \t-c\_K. In order to conclude the proof of assertion (1), we will apply Lemma to the subfield K_0 of K. In light of this, it suffices to show that the epsilon_t which appears in the argument above is independent of K(t) for t in K_0 which is strongly-general in K|k. With this in mind, suppose that u,t in K_0 are both strongly-general in K|k. Let epsilon_t resp. epsilon_u be as above, and assume for a contradiction that epsilon_t neq epsilon_u. Since the epsilon_t resp. epsilon_u depends only on K(t) resp. K(u) and tau, this implies that K(t) neq K(u), hence K(t) neq K(u) by Proposition . In particular, u,t are algebraically independent over k. By Proposition , there exists a non-empty open subset U of A^2_k such that (a,b) in U(k) implies that (t-a)/(u-b) is strongly-general in K|k. Moreover, since t,u are general in K|k, it follows that the sets \\t-a\_K\_a in k_0, \\u-a\_K\_a in k_0 are Z/ell-independent in k^M_1(K). Since k_0 is infinite, there exists some (a,b) in U(k_0) such that \t-a\_K and \u-b\_K are Z/ell-independent in k^M_1(K). Put x = (t-a)/(u-b), and recall that x in K_0 and that x is strongly-general in K|k. Let epsilon_x be again as above. Now we calculate, similarly to the proof of Proposition : \[epsilon_x cdot (\t-a\_K - \u-b\_K) = tauleft\fract-au-bright\_K = epsilon_t cdot \t-a\_K-epsilon_u cdot \u-b\_K.\] Since \t-a\_K and \u-b\_K are linearly-independent in k^M_1(K), it follows that epsilon_t = epsilon_x = epsilon_u. This concludes the proof of (1), and we let epsilon be the unique element of (Z/ell)^times such that tau\t\_K = epsilon cdot \t\_K for all t in K_0. I.e. epsilon = epsilon_t for some/all t in K_0 which is strongly-general in K|k. vskip 5pt noindentProof of (2): Let b in k be given, assume that t in K_0 is strongly-general in K|k, and let epsilon be as in the proof of (1) above. By Lemma , we see that tauV[t;infty] = V[t;infty]. Since V[t;b] neq V[t;infty], it follows that there exists a unique c in k such that tauV[t;b] = V[t;c]. Arguing similarly to the above, we have div_Psi(tau\t-b\_K) = div_Psi^tau(\t-b\_K) &= epsilon cdot [tauV[t;b]] - epsilon cdot [tauV[t;infty]] \\ &= epsilon cdot [V[t;c]] - epsilon cdot [V[t;infty]] \\ &= div_Psi(epsilon cdot \t-c\_K). The injectivity of div_Psi implies that tau\t-b\_K = epsilon cdot \t-c\_K, as required. Finally, the uniqueness of c follows from the fact that c mapsto V[t;c] : P^1(k) rightarrow D_t is a bijection, and that c is uniquely determined by the condition that tauV[t;b] = V[t;c].

  \begin{enumerate}
    \item First, $\tau \mathfrak{K}(t) = \mathfrak{K}(t)$ by Lemma \ref{lemma: mainproof / K0 / fix-Kfrakt0}.
    \item Second, one has $\tau \mathfrak{V} \in \mathfrak{D}_t$ for all $\mathfrak{V} \in \mathfrak{D}_t$ by Lemma \ref{lemma: mainproof / K0 / divs-local-thy} and the definition of $\mathfrak{D}_t$.
    \item Third, for all $c \in k_0 \cup \{\infty\} = \mathbb{P}^1(k_0)$, one has $\tau\mathfrak{V}[t;c] = \mathfrak{V}[t;c]$ by Lemma \ref{lemma: mainproof / K0 / fix-K0-strgen-divs}.
  \end{enumerate}
  In particular, $\tau$ induces isomorphisms $\tau : \mathfrak{K}(t)/\mathfrak{V} \xrightarrow{\cong} \mathfrak{K}(t)/\tau\mathfrak{V}$ for every $\mathfrak{V} \in \mathfrak{D}_t$.

  Let $\Psi = (\Psi_{\mathfrak{V}})_{\mathfrak{V} \in \mathfrak{D}_t}$ be the canonical rational-like collection associated to $\mathbb{K}(t)|k$, as defined in \S\ref{subsection: strgen / rational-like}.
  Consider the induced rational-like collection $\Psi^\tau = (\Psi^\tau_{\mathfrak{V}})_{\mathfrak{V} \in \mathfrak{D}_t}$, where the isomorphism $\Psi^\tau_{\tau\mathfrak{V}} : \mathfrak{K}(t)/\tau\mathfrak{V} \xrightarrow{\cong}\mathbb{Z}/\ell$ indexed by $\tau\mathfrak{V}$ is the unique one making the following diagram commute:
  \[
  \xymatrix{
    \mathfrak{K}(t) \ar[d]_\tau \ar@{->>}[r] & \mathfrak{K}(t)/\mathfrak{V} \ar[d]_\tau \ar[r]^-{\Psi_{\mathfrak{V}}} & \mathbb{Z}/\ell \ar@{=}[d] \\
    \mathfrak{K}(t) \ar@{->>}[r] & \mathfrak{K}(t)/\tau\mathfrak{V} \ar[r]_-{\Psi^\tau_{\tau\mathfrak{V}}} & \mathbb{Z}/\ell.
  }
  \]
  By Lemma \ref{lemma: strgen / rational-like / rational-like}, there exists an $\epsilon_t \in (\mathbb{Z}/\ell)^\times$ such that $\epsilon_t \cdot \Psi_{\tau\mathfrak{V}} = \Psi^\tau_{\tau\mathfrak{V}}$ for all $\mathfrak{V} \in \mathfrak{D}_t$.
  Since it will be used later on, recall that this $\epsilon_t$ only depends on $\mathfrak{K}(t)$ and $\tau$.
  
  \vskip 5pt
  \noindent\emph{Proof of (1):} 
  Now let $c \in k_0$ be given.
  Then one has $\mathrm{div}_\Psi(\{t-c\}_K) = [\mathfrak{V}[t;c]] - [\mathfrak{V}[t;\infty]]$ since $\Psi$ is the canonical rational-like collection associated to $\mathbb{K}(t)$.
  
  By Lemma \ref{lemma: mainproof / K0 / fix-K0-strgen-divs}, one has $\tau\mathfrak{V}[t;c] = \mathfrak{V}[t;c]$ and $\tau\mathfrak{V}[t;\infty] = \mathfrak{V}[t;\infty]$.
  And since $\Psi^\tau_{\tau\mathfrak{V}} = \epsilon_t \cdot \Psi_{\tau\mathfrak{V}}$ for all $\mathfrak{V} \in \mathfrak{D}_t$, we deduce that
  \[ \mathrm{div}_\Psi(\tau\{t-c\}_K) = \mathrm{div}_{\Psi^\tau}(\{t-c\}_K) = \epsilon_t \cdot [\mathfrak{V}[t;c]] - \epsilon_t \cdot [\mathfrak{V}[t;\infty]] = \mathrm{div}_\Psi(\epsilon_t \cdot \{t-c\}_K). \]
  The injectivity of $\mathrm{div}_\Psi$ implies that $\tau\{t-c\}_K = \epsilon_t \cdot \{t-c\}_K$.

  In order to conclude the proof of assertion (1), we will apply Lemma \ref{lemma: strgen / strgen / strgen-generate} to the subfield $K_0$ of $K$.
  In light of this, it suffices to show that the $\epsilon_t$ which appears in the argument above is independent of $\mathfrak{K}(t)$ for $t \in K_0$ which is strongly-general in $K|k$.

  With this in mind, suppose that $u,t \in K_0$ are both strongly-general in $K|k$.
  Let $\epsilon_t$ resp. $\epsilon_u$ be as above, and assume for a contradiction that $\epsilon_t \neq \epsilon_u$.
  Since the $\epsilon_t$ resp. $\epsilon_u$ depends only on $\mathfrak{K}(t)$ resp. $\mathfrak{K}(u)$ and $\tau$, this implies that $\mathfrak{K}(t) \neq \mathfrak{K}(u)$, hence $\mathbb{K}(t) \neq \mathbb{K}(u)$ by Proposition \ref{proposition: lattice / mod-ell / mod-ell-lattice}.
  In particular, $u,t$ are algebraically independent over $k$.

  By Proposition \ref{proposition: strgen / strgen / strgen-birat-bertini}, there exists a non-empty open subset $U$ of $\mathbb{A}^2_k$ such that $(a,b) \in U(k)$ implies that $(t-a)/(u-b)$ is strongly-general in $K|k$.
  Moreover, since $t,u$ are general in $K|k$, it follows that the sets $\{\{t-a\}_K\}_{a \in k_0}$, $\{\{u-a\}_K\}_{a \in k_0}$ are $\mathbb{Z}/\ell$-independent in $\operatorname{k}^{\rm M}_1(K)$.
  Since $k_0$ is infinite, there exists some $(a,b) \in U(k_0)$ such that $\{t-a\}_K$ and $\{u-b\}_K$ are $\mathbb{Z}/\ell$-independent in $\operatorname{k}^{\rm M}_1(K)$.

  Put $x = (t-a)/(u-b)$, and recall that $x \in K_0$ and that $x$ is strongly-general in $K|k$.
  Let $\epsilon_x$ be again as above.
  Now we calculate, similarly to the proof of Proposition \ref{proposition: strgen / rational-like / ident-criterion}:
  \[\epsilon_x \cdot (\{t-a\}_K - \{u-b\}_K) = \tau\left\{\frac{t-a}{u-b}\right\}_K = \epsilon_t \cdot \{t-a\}_K-\epsilon_u \cdot \{u-b\}_K.\]
  Since $\{t-a\}_K$ and $\{u-b\}_K$ are linearly-independent in $\operatorname{k}^{\rm M}_1(K)$, it follows that $\epsilon_t = \epsilon_x = \epsilon_u$.
  This concludes the proof of (1), and we let $\epsilon$ be the unique element of $(\mathbb{Z}/\ell)^\times$ such that $\tau\{t\}_K = \epsilon \cdot \{t\}_K$ for all $t \in K_0$.
  I.e. $\epsilon = \epsilon_t$ for some/all $t \in K_0$ which is strongly-general in $K|k$.

  \vskip 5pt
  \noindent\emph{Proof of (2):} Let $b \in k$ be given, assume that $t \in K_0$ is strongly-general in $K|k$, and let $\epsilon$ be as in the proof of (1) above.
  By Lemma \ref{lemma: mainproof / K0 / fix-K0-strgen-divs}, we see that $\tau\mathfrak{V}[t;\infty] = \mathfrak{V}[t;\infty]$.
  Since $\mathfrak{V}[t;b] \neq \mathfrak{V}[t;\infty]$, it follows that there exists a unique $c \in k$ such that $\tau\mathfrak{V}[t;b] = \mathfrak{V}[t;c]$.
  Arguing similarly to the above, we have
  \begin{align*}
    \mathrm{div}_{\Psi}(\tau\{t-b\}_K) = \mathrm{div}_{\Psi^\tau}(\{t-b\}_K) &= \epsilon \cdot [\tau\mathfrak{V}[t;b]] - \epsilon \cdot [\tau\mathfrak{V}[t;\infty]] \\
                  &= \epsilon \cdot [\mathfrak{V}[t;c]] - \epsilon \cdot [\mathfrak{V}[t;\infty]] \\
                  &= \mathrm{div}_\Psi(\epsilon \cdot \{t-c\}_K).
  \end{align*}
  The injectivity of $\mathrm{div}_\Psi$ implies that $\tau\{t-b\}_K = \epsilon \cdot \{t-c\}_K$, as required.
  Finally, the uniqueness of $c$ follows from the fact that $c \mapsto \mathfrak{V}[t;c] : \mathbb{P}^1(k) \rightarrow \mathfrak{D}_t$ is a bijection, and that $c$ is uniquely determined by the condition that $\tau\mathfrak{V}[t;b] = \mathfrak{V}[t;c]$.

nodes.statement: For f_1,ldots,f_s in k[x,y], we denote by V(f_1,ldots,f_s) the (reduced) closed subvariety of A^2_x,y given by the ideal sqrt(f_1,ldots,f_s). We will abuse the notation, and also write V(f_1,ldots,f_r) for the closure of this subvariety in P^2_x,y, also considered as a (reduced) subvariety. Following our notational conventions, we denote the closed points of P^2_x,y by their associated k-rational point, written in homogeneous coordinates. In particular, the closed points of A^2_x,y are written as (1:a_1:a_2), a_1,a_2 in k, and the points of P^2_x,y smallsetminus A^2_x,y are written as (0:a_1:a_2), a_1,a_2 in k, (a_1,a_2) neq (0,0). Let v denote the divisorial valuation of k(x,y)|k associated to the prime Weil-divisor Z := P^2_x,y smallsetminus A^2_x,y on P^2_x,y. For any a in k, let v_a be the 2-divisorial valuation of k(x,y)|k refining v which is associated to the rational point (0:a:1) on Z. Thus (v,v_a) is a flag of divisorial valuations of k(x,y)|k of length 2. Let eta denote the generic point of Z. To simplify the exposition later in the proof, we will say that a in k is allowable if the fiber of X rightarrow P^2_x,y over the point (0:a:1) is non-empty and essentially unramified in K. Since (0:b:1) lies on Z, assumptions (1) and (3) imply that the fiber X_eta of X rightarrow P^2_x,y over eta is non-empty and essentially unramified in K. Therefore, we see that all but finitely many a in k (including b) are allowable. For h in k, we write t_h := (x-h)/y. We also write t := t_0 = x/y. Note that for all a in k, the system (1/x,t-a) is a system of regular parameters for the regular closed point (0:a:1), and the flag of divisorial valuations associated to this system is precisely (v,v_a). Thus, by the discussion of S and using Fact , we see that there exists an ell-unramified prolongation w of v to K. In other words, w is a divisorial valuation of K|k which prolongs v, and the canonical map \[ k^M_1(k(x,y))/\U_v\_k(x,y) rightarrow k^M_1(K)/U_w cong Z/ell \] is an isomorphism. Using the same argument, for any allowable a in k, there exists an ell-unramified prolongation w_a of v_a to K which refines w. In other words, for such a in k, w_a is a 2-divisorial valuation of K|k which refines w and prolongs v_a, and one has a canonical isomorphism \[ \U_v\_k(x,y)/\U_v_a\_k(x,y) rightarrow U_w/U_w_a. \] Note also that one has \t_h-a\_k(x,y) in \U_v\_k(x,y)smallsetminus\U_v_a\_k(x,y) for all h in k. To summarize, for any allowable a in k, the flag (w,w_a) is an ell-unramified prolongation of (v,v_a) to K, and the following conditions hold: item One has \1/x\_K in k^M_1(K) smallsetminus U_w hence \x\_K in k^M_1(K) smallsetminus U_w. item For all h in k, one has \t_h-a\_K in U_w smallsetminus U_w_a. By Lemma , there exists a unique divisorial valuation w^sigma of K|k, and for every allowable a in k as above, there exists a unique 2-divisorial valuation w_a^sigma of K|k, such that the following conditions hold: item w_a^sigma refines w^sigma. item sigmaU_w = U_w^sigma and sigma U_w^1 = U_w^sigma^1. item sigmaU_w_a = U_w_a^sigma and sigma U_w_a^1 = U_w_a^sigma^1. Finally, we let v^sigma resp. v_a^sigma be the restrictions of w^sigma resp. w_a^sigma to k(x,y). One has v^sigma = v. Recall that eta denotes the generic point of Z in P^2_x,y. As P^2_x,y is proper over k, the valuation v^sigma has a unique center on P^2_x,y. Since eta is a regular codimension 1 point of P^2_x,y, it suffices to show that the center of v^sigma on P^2_x,y is eta. Recall that one has sigma\x\_K = \x\_K by Proposition , and that sigmaU_w = U_w^sigma as noted above. Since \x\_K notin U_w, we see that \[ \x\_K = sigma \x\_K notin U_w^sigma. \] In particular, v^sigma(x) neq 0. This implies that the center of v^sigma on P^2_x,y is contained in the support of the function x, which is V(x) cup Z. On the other hand, note that one also has \x-1\_k(x,y) notin \U_v\_k(x,y), hence \x-1\_K is also a generator of k^M_1(K)/U_w. By repeating the same argument with x-1 in place of x, and noting that sigma\x-1\_K = \x-1\_K by Proposition , we deduce that the center of v^sigma on P^2_x,y must actually be contained in Z, since the support of x-1 on P^2_x,y is V(x-1) cup Z. Now assume for a contradiction that the center of v^sigma is a closed point P on Z. For an allowable a in k, recall that v_a^sigma refines v. It therefore follows that the center of v_a^sigma on P^2_x,y must also be this closed point P. Now let a_0 in k_0 be allowable -- such an a_0 exists since k_0 is infinite. By Proposition , we have \t-a_0\_K = sigma\t-a_0\_K. Therefore \t-a_0\_K notin U_w_a_0^sigma, hence v_a_0^sigma(t-a_0) neq 0. By considering the support of t-a_0 in P^2_x,y, we see that the point P must be either the point (0:a_0:1) or the point (0:1:0). In fact, it follows that P must be the point (0:1:0) since we can repeat this argument with a different allowable a_1 in k_0, a_1 neq a_0, which exists since k_0 is infinite. Now consider the function (t-a_0)/(t-a_1) for a_1 in k_0 distinct from a_0. By Proposition , we have \(t-a_0)/(t-a_1)\_K = sigma\(t-a_0)/(t-a_1)\_K, while \t-a_1\_K in U_w_a_0. Therefore, \(t-a_0)/(t-a_1)\_K notin U_w_a_0^sigma, hence v_a_0^sigma((t-a_0)/(t-a_1)) neq 0. By looking at the support of (t-a_0)/(t-a_1) on P^2_x,y, we obtain a contradiction to the fact that P = (0:1:0). Having obtained our contradiction, it follows that the center of v^sigma cannot be a closed point on Z. This means that the center of v^sigma must be the generic point of Z, which concludes the proof of the claim. Recall from Proposition (2) that there exist unique constants b_e,b_f in k such that sigma\t_e-b\_K = \t_e-b_e\_K and sigma\t_f-b\_K = \t_f-b_f\_K. We must show that b_e = b_f. Note that one has \t_e-b\_K in U_w smallsetminus U_w_b, so that by Proposition , we have \[ \t_e-b_e\_K in U_w^sigma smallsetminus U_w_b^sigma. \] In particular, v_b^sigma is a proper refinement of v^sigma. Thus, the center Q of v_b^sigma on P^2_x,y must be a closed point on the line Z at infinity, for otherwise this center would be eta which would imply that v^sigma = v^sigma_b by the claim above. Let a in k_0 be different from b. By Proposition , we see that sigma\(t_e-b)/(t_e-a)\_K = \(t_e-b_e)/(t_e-a)\_K, and thus \[ \(t_e-b_e)/(t_e-a)\_K notin U_w_b^sigma. \] By considering the support of the function (t_e-b_e)/(t_e-a) on P^2_x,y, it follows that Q cannot be the point (0:1:0). Thus, this center Q must be a point of the form (0:c:1) for some c in k. Recalling that \[ \t_e-b_e\_K in U_w^sigma smallsetminus U_w_b^sigma\] so that v_b^sigma(t_e-b_e) neq 0, we deduce from this that b_e = c. Finally, by noting that also \[ \t_f-b_f\_K in U_w^sigma smallsetminus U_w_b^sigma, \] we deduce similarly that b_f = c. Thus, one has c = b_e = b_f, as required.

  We will abuse the notation, and also write $V(f_1,\ldots,f_r)$ for the closure of this subvariety in $\mathbb{P}^2_{x,y}$, also considered as a (reduced) subvariety.
  Following our notational conventions, we denote the closed points of $\mathbb{P}^2_{x,y}$ by their associated $k$-rational point, written in homogeneous coordinates.
  In particular, the closed points of $\mathbb{A}^2_{x,y}$ are written as $(1:a_1:a_2)$, $a_1,a_2 \in k$, and the points of $\mathbb{P}^2_{x,y} \smallsetminus \mathbb{A}^2_{x,y}$ are written as $(0:a_1:a_2)$, $a_1,a_2 \in k$, $(a_1,a_2) \neq (0,0)$.

  Let $v$ denote the divisorial valuation of $k(x,y)|k$ associated to the prime Weil-divisor $Z := \mathbb{P}^2_{x,y} \smallsetminus \mathbb{A}^2_{x,y}$ on $\mathbb{P}^2_{x,y}$.
  For any $a \in k$, let $v_a$ be the $2$-divisorial valuation of $k(x,y)|k$ refining $v$ which is associated to the rational point $(0:a:1)$ on $Z$.
  Thus $(v,v_a)$ is a flag of divisorial valuations of $k(x,y)|k$ of length $2$.

  Let $\eta$ denote the generic point of $Z$.
  To simplify the exposition later in the proof, we will say that $a \in k$ is {\bf allowable} if the fiber of $X \rightarrow \mathbb{P}^2_{x,y}$ over the point $(0:a:1)$ is non-empty and essentially unramified in $K$.
  Since $(0:b:1)$ lies on $Z$, assumptions (1) and (3) imply that the fiber $X_\eta$ of $X \rightarrow \mathbb{P}^2_{x,y}$ over $\eta$ is non-empty and essentially unramified in $K$.
  Therefore, we see that all but finitely many $a \in k$ (including $b$) are allowable.

  For $h \in k$, we write $t_h := (x-h)/y$.
  We also write $t := t_0 = x/y$.
  Note that for all $a \in k$, the system $(1/x,t-a)$ is a system of regular parameters for the regular closed point $(0:a:1)$, and the flag of divisorial valuations associated to this system is precisely $(v,v_a)$.
  Thus, by the discussion of \S\ref{subsection: essram / essential-unram} and using Fact \ref{fact: essram / essential-branch-locus / essential-branch-fact}, we see that there exists an $\ell$-unramified prolongation $w$ of $v$ to $K$.
  In other words, $w$ is a divisorial valuation of $K|k$ which prolongs $v$, and the canonical map
  \[ \operatorname{k}^{\rm M}_1(k(x,y))/\{{\rm U}_v\}_{k(x,y)} \rightarrow \operatorname{k}^{\rm M}_1(K)/\mathfrak{U}_w \cong \mathbb{Z}/\ell \]
  is an isomorphism.
  Using the same argument, for any allowable $a \in k$, there exists an $\ell$-unramified prolongation $w_a$ of $v_a$ to $K$ which \emph{refines} $w$.
  In other words, for such $a \in k$, $w_a$ is a $2$-divisorial valuation of $K|k$ which refines $w$ and prolongs $v_a$, and one has a canonical isomorphism
  \[ \{{\rm U}_v\}_{k(x,y)}/\{{\rm U}_{v_a}\}_{k(x,y)} \rightarrow \mathfrak{U}_w/\mathfrak{U}_{w_a}. \]
  Note also that one has $\{t_h-a\}_{k(x,y)} \in \{{\rm U}_v\}_{k(x,y)}\smallsetminus\{{\rm U}_{v_a}\}_{k(x,y)}$ for all $h \in k$.
  To summarize, for any allowable $a \in k$, the flag $(w,w_a)$ is an $\ell$-unramified prolongation of $(v,v_a)$ to $K$, and the following conditions hold:
  \begin{enumerate}
    \item One has $\{1/x\}_K \in \operatorname{k}^{\rm M}_1(K) \smallsetminus \mathfrak{U}_w$ hence $\{x\}_K \in \operatorname{k}^{\rm M}_1(K) \smallsetminus \mathfrak{U}_w$.
    \item For all $h \in k$, one has $\{t_h-a\}_K \in \mathfrak{U}_w \smallsetminus \mathfrak{U}_{w_a}$.
  \end{enumerate}

  By Lemma \ref{lemma: mainproof / K0 / divs-local-thy}, there exists a unique divisorial valuation $w^\sigma$ of $K|k$, and for every allowable $a \in k$ as above, there exists a unique $2$-divisorial valuation $w_a^\sigma$ of $K|k$, such that the following conditions hold:
  \begin{enumerate}
    \item $w_a^\sigma$ refines $w^\sigma$.
    \item $\sigma\mathfrak{U}_w = \mathfrak{U}_{w^\sigma}$ and $\sigma \mathfrak{U}_w^1 = \mathfrak{U}_{w^\sigma}^1$.
    \item $\sigma\mathfrak{U}_{w_a} = \mathfrak{U}_{w_a^\sigma}$ and $\sigma \mathfrak{U}_{w_a}^1 = \mathfrak{U}_{w_a^\sigma}^1$.
  \end{enumerate}
  Finally, we let $v^\sigma$ resp. $v_a^\sigma$ be the restrictions of $w^\sigma$ resp. $w_a^\sigma$ to $k(x,y)$.

  \begin{claim*}
    One has $v^\sigma = v$.
  \end{claim*}
  \begin{proof}
    Recall that $\eta$ denotes the generic point of $Z$ in $\mathbb{P}^2_{x,y}$.
    As $\mathbb{P}^2_{x,y}$ is proper over $k$, the valuation $v^\sigma$ has a unique center on $\mathbb{P}^2_{x,y}$.
    Since $\eta$ is a regular codimension $1$ point of $\mathbb{P}^2_{x,y}$, it suffices to show that the center of $v^\sigma$ on $\mathbb{P}^2_{x,y}$ is $\eta$.

    Recall that one has $\sigma\{x\}_K = \{x\}_K$ by Proposition \ref{proposition: mainproof / K0 / fix-K0}, and that $\sigma\mathfrak{U}_w = \mathfrak{U}_{w^\sigma}$ as noted above.
    Since $\{x\}_K \notin \mathfrak{U}_w$, we see that
    \[ \{x\}_K = \sigma \{x\}_K \notin \mathfrak{U}_{w^\sigma}. \]
    In particular, $v^\sigma(x) \neq 0$.
    This implies that the center of $v^\sigma$ on $\mathbb{P}^2_{x,y}$ is contained in the support of the function $x$, which is $V(x) \cup Z$.

    On the other hand, note that one also has $\{x-1\}_{k(x,y)} \notin \{{\rm U}_v\}_{k(x,y)}$, hence $\{x-1\}_K$ is also a generator of $\operatorname{k}^{\rm M}_1(K)/\mathfrak{U}_w$.
    By repeating the same argument with $x-1$ in place of $x$, and noting that $\sigma\{x-1\}_K = \{x-1\}_K$ by Proposition \ref{proposition: mainproof / K0 / fix-K0}, we deduce that the center of $v^\sigma$ on $\mathbb{P}^2_{x,y}$ must actually be contained in $Z$, since the support of $x-1$ on $\mathbb{P}^2_{x,y}$ is $V(x-1) \cup Z$.

    Now assume for a contradiction that the center of $v^\sigma$ is a closed point $P$ on $Z$.
    For an allowable $a \in k$, recall that $v_a^\sigma$ refines $v$.
    It therefore follows that the center of $v_a^\sigma$ on $\mathbb{P}^2_{x,y}$ must also be this closed point $P$.

    Now let $a_0 \in k_0$ be allowable -- such an $a_0$ exists since $k_0$ is infinite.
    By Proposition \ref{proposition: mainproof / K0 / fix-K0}, we have $\{t-a_0\}_K = \sigma\{t-a_0\}_K$.
    Therefore $\{t-a_0\}_K \notin \mathfrak{U}_{w_{a_0}^\sigma}$, hence $v_{a_0}^\sigma(t-a_0) \neq 0$.
    By considering the support of $t-a_0$ in $\mathbb{P}^2_{x,y}$, we see that the point $P$ must be either the point $(0:a_0:1)$ or the point $(0:1:0)$.
    In fact, it follows that $P$ must be the point $(0:1:0)$ since we can repeat this argument with a different allowable $a_1 \in k_0$, $a_1 \neq a_0$, which exists since $k_0$ is infinite.

    Now consider the function $(t-a_0)/(t-a_1)$ for $a_1 \in k_0$ distinct from $a_0$.
    By Proposition \ref{proposition: mainproof / K0 / fix-K0}, we have $\{(t-a_0)/(t-a_1)\}_K = \sigma\{(t-a_0)/(t-a_1)\}_K$, while $\{t-a_1\}_K \in \mathfrak{U}_{w_{a_0}}$.
    Therefore, $\{(t-a_0)/(t-a_1)\}_K \notin \mathfrak{U}_{w_{a_0}^\sigma}$, hence $v_{a_0}^\sigma((t-a_0)/(t-a_1)) \neq 0$.
    By looking at the support of $(t-a_0)/(t-a_1)$ on $\mathbb{P}^2_{x,y}$, we obtain a contradiction to the fact that $P = (0:1:0)$.

    Having obtained our contradiction, it follows that the center of $v^\sigma$ cannot be a closed point on $Z$.
    This means that the center of $v^\sigma$ must be the generic point of $Z$, which concludes the proof of the claim.
  \end{proof}

  Recall from Proposition \ref{proposition: mainproof / K0 / fix-K0}(2) that there exist unique constants $b_e,b_f \in k$ such that $\sigma\{t_e-b\}_K = \{t_e-b_e\}_K$ and $\sigma\{t_f-b\}_K = \{t_f-b_f\}_K$.
  We must show that $b_e = b_f$.

  Note that one has $\{t_e-b\}_K \in \mathfrak{U}_w \smallsetminus \mathfrak{U}_{w_b}$, so that by Proposition \ref{proposition: mainproof / K0 / fix-K0}, we have
  \[ \{t_e-b_e\}_K \in \mathfrak{U}_{w^\sigma} \smallsetminus \mathfrak{U}_{w_b^\sigma}. \]
  In particular, $v_b^\sigma$ is a proper refinement of $v^\sigma$.
  Thus, the center $Q$ of $v_b^\sigma$ on $\mathbb{P}^2_{x,y}$ must be a closed point on the line $Z$ at infinity, for otherwise this center would be $\eta$ which would imply that $v^\sigma = v^\sigma_b$ by the claim above.

  Let $a \in k_0$ be different from $b$.
  By Proposition \ref{proposition: mainproof / K0 / fix-K0}, we see that $\sigma\{(t_e-b)/(t_e-a)\}_K = \{(t_e-b_e)/(t_e-a)\}_K$, and thus
  \[ \{(t_e-b_e)/(t_e-a)\}_K \notin \mathfrak{U}_{w_b^\sigma}. \]
  By considering the support of the function $(t_e-b_e)/(t_e-a)$ on $\mathbb{P}^2_{x,y}$, it follows that $Q$ cannot be the point $(0:1:0)$.
  Thus, this center $Q$ must be a point of the form $(0:c:1)$ for some $c \in k$.
  Recalling that
  \[ \{t_e-b_e\}_K \in \mathfrak{U}_{w^\sigma} \smallsetminus \mathfrak{U}_{w_b^\sigma}\]
  so that $v_b^\sigma(t_e-b_e) \neq 0$, we deduce from this that $b_e = c$.
  Finally, by noting that also
  \[ \{t_f-b_f\}_K \in \mathfrak{U}_{w^\sigma} \smallsetminus \mathfrak{U}_{w_b^\sigma}, \]
  we deduce similarly that $b_f = c$.
  Thus, one has $c = b_e = b_f$, as required.

By Lemma (1), for all but finitely many a in k, the field K' is regular over F(t_1+a cdot t_3); since k_0 is infinite, we may choose such an a which lies in k_0. Applying Lemma (1) again, for all but finitely many b in k, the field K' is regular over F(t_1 + a cdot t_3,t_2 + b cdot t_3); again, we may choose such a b which lies in k_0. We put x = t_1 + a cdot t_3 and y = t_2 + b cdot t_3 for a,b in k_0 as above. Next, put F_1 = F(x), F_2 = F(y) and F_12 = F(x,y), and note that F_* is relatively algebraically closed in K' for * = 1,2,12. Also, for * = 1,2,12, let M_* denote the relative algebraic closure of F_* in K. Since K|K' is purely-inseparable, the extension M_*|F_* is also purely-inseparable.   Note that $K'$ is then a regular extension of $F$.
  By Lemma \ref{lemma: strgen / general / gen-birat-bertini}(1), for all but finitely many $a \in k$, the field $K'$ is regular over $F(t_1+a \cdot t_3)$; since $k_0$ is infinite, we may choose such an $a$ which lies in $k_0$.

  \[ \mathbb{A}^3_{t_1,t_2,t_3} \rightarrow \mathbb{P}^2_{x,y}, \]

  is a (regular) smooth surjective morphism with geometrically integral fibers.
  Moreover, the point $P = (a_1,\ldots,a_d)$ is contained in the closure of every fiber of $X \rightarrow \mathbb{P}^2_{x,y}$.
  Since $P$ is essentially unramified in $K$, it follows that all the fibers of $X \rightarrow \mathbb{P}^2_{x,y}$ must be essentially unramified in $K$.

Put $K = k(X)$ for some $X \in \mathcal{U}_2$ and $L = k(Y)$ for some $Y \in \mathcal{U}_1$.
  Since $\mathcal{U}_1$ dominates $\mathcal{U}_2$ in $\mathcal{V}$, we see that $K$ is a subfield of $L$.
  \vskip 5pt
  \noindent\emph{Proof of (1):}
  Arguing as in \S\ref{subsection: finalproof / ion-main-opens}, it suffices to show that the image of $\phi$ under the map
  \[ \mathrm{Aut}^{\rm c}(\pi^a|_{\mathcal{V}}) \rightarrow \mathrm{Aut}^{\rm c}(\pi^a|_{\mathcal{U}_2}) \hookrightarrow \mathrm{Aut}^{\rm c}(\mathcal{G}_K^a) \]
  is defined by $\tau$.
  Let $\phi_L$ resp. $\phi_K$ denote the image of $\phi$ in $\mathrm{Aut}^{\rm c}(\mathcal{G}_L^a)$ resp. $\mathrm{Aut}^{\rm c}(\mathcal{G}_K^a)$.
  Since $\phi|_{\mathcal{U}_1}$ is defined by $\tau$, we see that $\phi_L$ is defined by $\tau$ as well.
  
  Note that the assumptions of the lemma imply that $\phi_L$ and $\phi_K$ are compatible with the canonical morphism $\mathcal{G}_L^a \rightarrow \mathcal{G}_K^a$, i.e., the following diagram commutes:
  \[ 
  \xymatrix{
    \mathcal{G}_L^a \ar[d] \ar[r]^{\phi_L} & \mathcal{G}_L^a \ar[d] \\
    \mathcal{G}_K^a \ar[r]_{\phi_K} & \mathcal{G}_K^a.
  }
  \]
  We will now deal with the cases $\dim \mathcal{U}_2 \neq 1$ and $\dim \mathcal{U}_2 = 1$ separately.
  \vskip 5pt
  \noindent\underline{Case $\dim \mathcal{U}_2 = 1$:} In this case, our assumptions ensure that $\mathcal{G}_L^a \rightarrow \mathcal{G}_K^a$ is \emph{surjective}.
  Since $\phi_L$ is defined by $\tau$, and since $\phi_L$ and $\phi_K$ are compatible with the projection $\mathcal{G}_L^a \twoheadrightarrow \mathcal{G}_K^a$, it follows that $\phi_K$ must also be defined by $\tau$.

  \vskip 5pt
  \noindent\underline{Case $\dim \mathcal{U}_2 > 1:$} Let $\psi = \tau^{-1} \cdot \phi_K$ denote the composition of $\phi_K$ with the element of $\mathrm{Aut}^{\rm c}(\mathcal{G}_K^a)$ induced by $\tau^{-1}$.
  Furthermore, let $\psi^* \in \mathrm{Aut}^{\rm M}(\operatorname{k}^{\rm M}_1(K))$ be the element associated to $\psi$ via the Kummer pairing (see Theorem \ref{theorem: cohom / kummer / galois-to-milnor}).
  Finally, note that the image of $\mathcal{G}_L^a \rightarrow \mathcal{G}_K^a$ is an open subgroup of $\mathcal{G}_K^a$, on which $\psi$ acts as the identity.
  Thus, there exists a \emph{finite} subgroup $H_0$ of $\operatorname{k}^{\rm M}_1(K)$ such that for every $x \in \operatorname{k}^{\rm M}_1(K)$, one has $\psi^* x \in x + H_0$.
  Therefore, there is a subgroup $H$ of $\operatorname{k}^{\rm M}_1(K)$ such that $\psi^*$ acts as the identity on $H$, and such that $H$ has finite index in $\operatorname{k}^{\rm M}_1(K)$.

  We will show that $\psi^*$ is some $(\mathbb{Z}/\ell)^\times$-multiple of the identity on $\operatorname{k}^{\rm M}_1(K)$.
  First, suppose that $t \in K \smallsetminus k$ is given and consider the one-dimensional geometric subgroup $\mathfrak{K}(t)$.
  The inclusion $k(t) \hookrightarrow K$ induces a (possibly non-injective) map $\operatorname{k}^{\rm M}_1(k(t)) \rightarrow \operatorname{k}^{\rm M}_1(K)$ and we let $M$ denote the preimage of $H$ in $\operatorname{k}^{\rm M}_1(k(t))$.
  Since $H$ has finite index in $\operatorname{k}^{\rm M}_1(K)$, it follows that $M$ must have finite index in $\operatorname{k}^{\rm M}_1(k(t))$.

  \begin{claim*}
    There exists some $x \in k(t) \smallsetminus k$ such that $\{x-c\}_{k(t)} \in M$ for infinitely many $c \in k$.
  \end{claim*}
  \begin{proof}
    Since $M$ has finite index in $\operatorname{k}^{\rm M}_1(k(t))$, there exists some $f \in k(t)^\times$ such that the set 
    \[ \mathcal{S} := \{a \in k \ : \ \{f \cdot (t-a)\}_{k(t)} \in M\} \]
    is infinite.
    Note that for all $a,b \in \mathcal{S}$ one has $\{(t-a)/(t-b)\}_{k(t)} \in M$.
    Let $a,b \in \mathcal{S}$ be two different elements with $b \neq 0$.
    Put $x := (t-a)/(t-b)$, and let $c \in k$ be a constant such that $c \neq 1$.
    Since $\{1-c\}_{k(t)} = 0$, we find that
    \[ \{x-c\}_{k(t)} = \left\{\frac{t-a-ct+cb}{t-b}\right\}_{k(t)} = \left\{\frac{t-\frac{a-cb}{1-c}}{t-b}\right\}_{k(t)}.\]
    In particular, $\{x-c\}_{k(t)} \in M$ for every $c \in k \smallsetminus \{1\}$ such that $(a-cb)/(1-c) \in \mathcal{S}$.
    Since $\mathcal{S}$ was infinite, we see that there are infinitely many such constants $c$, which proves the claim.
  \end{proof}

  Let $x \in k(t) \smallsetminus k$ be as in the claim above.
  Then one has $\psi^*\{x-c\}_K = \{x-c\}_K$ for infinitely many $c \in k$.
  As $\mathfrak{K}(t) = \mathfrak{K}(x)$, it follows from Corollary \ref{corollary: milnorff / geometric / infinite-subsets} that $\psi^* \mathfrak{K}(t) = \mathfrak{K}(t)$.
  Finally, since $t \in K \smallsetminus k$ was arbitrary, Proposition \ref{proposition: strgen / rational-like / ident-criterion} shows that $\psi^* \in (\mathbb{Z}/\ell)^\times \cdot \mathbf{1}_{\operatorname{k}^{\rm M}_1(K)}$.
  In particular, $\psi = \tau^{-1} \cdot \phi_K$ is contained in $(\mathbb{Z}/\ell)^\times \cdot \mathbf{1}_{\mathcal{G}_K^a}$.

  Now note that we have a commutative diagram:
  \[ 
  \xymatrix{
    \mathcal{G}_L^a \ar[d] \ar@{=}[r] & \mathcal{G}_L^a \ar[d] \\
    \mathcal{G}_K^a \ar[r]_{\tau^{-1} \cdot \phi_K} & \mathcal{G}_K^a
  }
  \]
  and recall that the vertical arrows in this diagram have an open (hence non-trivial) image in $\mathcal{G}_K^a$.
  Since $\tau^{-1} \cdot \phi_K \in (\mathbb{Z}/\ell)^\times \cdot \mathbf{1}_{\mathcal{G}_K^a}$, it follows that $\tau^{-1} \cdot \phi_K = \mathbf{1}_{\mathcal{G}_K^a}$.
  This proves assertion (1).
  \vskip 5pt
  \noindent\emph{Proof of (2):}
  Recall that $\phi_K \in \mathrm{Aut}^{\rm c}(\mathcal{G}_K^a)$ is defined by $\tau$, and the assumption of (2) implies that $\epsilon \cdot \phi_K \in \mathrm{Aut}^{\rm c}(\mathcal{G}_K^a)$ is defined by $\tau'$.
  Since $\phi_K$ and $\epsilon \cdot \phi_K$ represent the same element of $\underline{\mathrm{Aut}}^{\rm c}(\mathcal{G}_K^a)$, and since one has a $\rho_{k_0}$-compatible isomorphism 
  \[ \underline{\mathrm{Aut}}^{\rm c}(\mathcal{G}_K^a) \cong \underline{\mathrm{Aut}}^{\rm M}(\operatorname{k}^{\rm M}_1(K)) \]
  by Theorem \ref{theorem: cohom / kummer / galois-to-milnor}, it follows from Lemma \ref{lemma: strgen / galois-action / faithfulness} that $\tau = \tau'$.
  Finally, since the map 
  \[ \rho_{k_0} : {\mathrm{Gal}_{k_0}} \rightarrow \mathrm{Aut}^{\rm c}(\mathcal{G}_K^a) \twoheadrightarrow \underline{\mathrm{Aut}}^{\rm c}(\mathcal{G}_K^a) \cong \underline{\mathrm{Aut}}^{\rm M}(\operatorname{k}^{\rm M}_1(K)) \]
  is injective by Lemma \ref{lemma: strgen / galois-action / faithfulness}, we see that $\epsilon = 1$, as required.
